**Why it matters (GS2 Health + IR).** This is India positioning its domestic delivery numbers as an exportable model of health diplomacy — the same play as vaccine diplomacy and the International Solar Alliance, but in public-health systems. For Mains, it is the cleanest recent illustration of "India as a norm-shaper in global health governance", and OneSCD gives sickle cell disease — long a neglected tropical-belt and tribal-health issue — a formal global platform for the first time.

**Key facts / figures presented by India:**

- Over **1.8 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs** functional across the country.
- Over **900 million citizens** hold unique digital health identities (ABHA, under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission).
- More than **497 million teleconsultations** delivered through **eSanjeevani**.
- **National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (launched 2018):** nearly **225 million beneficiaries screened**; services at about **1.80 lakh** primary healthcare facilities; **1,039** treatment centres. India is working to the WHO goal of **eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030**.
- **National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched 2023, target 2047):** **7.29 crore people screened**; over **20 lakh carriers** identified; **2.5 lakh** diagnosed; **4.93 crore Sickle Cell Cards** distributed.

**Destination notebook:** GS2 — Health/Governance and International Relations (India in global institutions).

articles.title: Ministry of Defence (Indian Navy): INS Trishul arrives at Toulon, France for the 24th edition of bilateral maritime Exercise VARUNA
articles.text:
**Issuing body:** Ministry of Defence / Indian Navy.

**What it is.** The Indian Navy's guided-missile frigate **INS Trishul** has arrived at **Toulon**, the principal base of the French Navy's Mediterranean fleet, for the **24th edition of Exercise VARUNA**. The engagement covers a harbour phase (cross-deck visits, professional exchanges, sporting fixtures) and a sea phase of operational drills.

**Why it matters (GS2 IR / GS3 Security).** VARUNA is the oldest continuous naval exercise in the India–France defence relationship, and France is one of only a handful of partners with which India holds exercises across all three services (VARUNA – navy, GARUDA – air force, SHAKTI – army). The deployment to the Mediterranean, rather than the Indian Ocean, signals an Indian Navy that is operating well beyond its immediate neighbourhood — relevant to any question on India's extended maritime reach and the Indo-Pacific–Mediterranean linkage.

**Key facts / figures:**

- **24th edition**; the India–France bilateral naval exercise began in **1993** and was christened **VARUNA** in **2001**.
- Venue: **Toulon**, southern France (Mediterranean).
- Participating Indian unit: **INS Trishul**, a guided-missile frigate.
- India–France trilateral: the two also run a trilateral format with the **UAE**, and cooperate in the Indian Ocean through France's territories (Réunion, Mayotte) and the **Indian Ocean Commission**, where India is an observer.

**Destination notebook:** GS2 — International Relations (bilateral: India–France); GS3 — Internal/External Security (defence exercises).

articles.title: Exercise 'Veer Guardian 2026' concludes at Jodhpur — and Japanese F-2s fly from Indian soil for the first time — International Relations
articles.text:
**Headline:** The India–Japan bilateral air exercise **Veer Guardian 2026** concluded at **Air Force Station Jodhpur** on **22 September 2026** — the **second edition** of the series, and the first held in India.

**Exam angle:**
- The direction of travel is what matters. The maiden edition (January 2023) was hosted at **Hyakuri Air Base, Japan**; hosting the second in India means the JASDF deployed fighters abroad to an Indian base — a reciprocity that only a handful of India's partners have. For a country whose Article 9 constitution constrained overseas military activity for decades, Japanese fighter deployments abroad are themselves a data point about Japan's security normalisation.
- Note what the exercise practised: **within-visual-range (WVR) air combat** and coordinated multi-aircraft operations — i.e. tactical interoperability, not a symbolic flypast. The **LCA Tejas** flying alongside the F-2 is the indigenisation subplot: the two air chiefs flew together in a Tejas on Distinguished Visitors' Day.
- Place it in the architecture, because UPSC tests the framework, not the exercise name. India–Japan is a **"Special Strategic and Global Partnership"**, serviced by an **Annual Summit**, a **2+2 Ministerial Dialogue**, and the **Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement (ACSA, 2020)** — a logistics-sharing pact of the same family as LEMOA (US), and the enabler that makes deployments like this practical.

**Facts to memorise:**
- **Veer Guardian**: India–Japan **air** exercise. 1st edition **January 2023, Hyakuri Air Base, Japan**; 2nd edition **September 2026, AFS Jodhpur**, concluded **22 September 2026**.
- Assets: **Japan — Mitsubishi F-2** (3 aircraft, 8th Wing, ~110 personnel); **India — Su-30MKI, Rafale, LCA Tejas**.
- Full India–Japan exercise set for the table: **Veer Guardian** (air), **Dharma Guardian** (army — recent edition at Chaubatia, Uttarakhand), **JIMEX** (navy, bilateral), **Malabar** (navy, with the US and Australia — Quad navies), **MILAN** (multilateral, Indian-hosted).
- Framework: Special Strategic and Global Partnership; **2+2 Ministerial**; **ACSA (2020)**; cooperation threads on **UNICORN** integrated mast (via BEL), DRDO–ATLA R&D, maritime domain awareness.

**Notebook:** GS2 — International Relations (India and bilateral/regional groupings; Indo-Pacific).

**Static anchor:** Your **India–Japan** bilateral note. Build (or complete) the **"Exercises with India" master table** — one row per partner country, columns for army/navy/air exercise names — this is the single highest-frequency Prelims factual grid in IR. Cross-link to the **logistics-agreements row**: LEMOA (US, 2016), ACSA (Japan, 2020), MLSA (Australia, 2020), and the France, Singapore and ROK agreements. Also cross-link to **Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution** and Japan's 2022 National Security Strategy in the Mains "Japan's security normalisation" box.

articles.title: Green nod for ports now lasts 20 years — and can stretch to 30 — Environment
articles.text:
**Headline:** On **22 September 2026**, the Environment Ministry amended the **EIA Notification, 2006** to raise the validity of prior environmental clearance for **ports, harbours, breakwaters and dredging** projects from **10 years (+1)** to **20 years**, extendable by **two further blocks of 5 years** — a possible **30-year** total.

**Exam angle:**
- This is the cleanest available illustration of the standing Mains tension: **regulatory certainty versus regulatory dilution**. The Ministry's stated ground is that port and harbour projects have "long gestation periods and phased development"; the Sectoral Expert Appraisal Committee held that 10+1 years was insufficient. The counter-argument writes itself — a clearance is an appraisal of *predicted* impacts against a *baseline*, and coastal baselines (sediment transport, shoreline, turtle nesting, mangrove cover, fisher livelihoods) move faster than 20 years. Longer validity means a project can be built against science two decades old, without re-appraisal.
- Watch the drafting detail, which is exactly the kind of specificity that earns marks: the final amendment inserts a **new paragraph 9(iva)** modelled on the **mining** provisions, rather than amending paras 9(ii)(b), 9(ii)(c) and the proviso to 9(iii) as the **May 2026 draft** had proposed. And the final term — **20 years** — is *longer* than the draft's 15, i.e. post-consultation the period went up, not down. That is a process point worth a line in an answer.
- The political overlay: **Jairam Ramesh** alleged the amendment was tailored to the **Great Nicobar Island** transshipment port. You do not need to adjudicate that; you need to note that project-specific criticism of a general notification is a recurring feature of Indian environmental regulation, and that **Great Nicobar** (Galathea Bay, leatherback turtles, Shompen and Nicobarese tribal reserve land) is a live case study you should already have on file.

**Facts to memorise:**
- Amendment to the **EIA Notification, 2006** (framed under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**), notified **22 September 2026**.
- Categories covered: **ports, harbours, breakwaters, dredging**. Old: **10 years + 1-year extension**. New: **20 years**, plus a **5-year** extension on EAC examination, plus a further **5 years** in deserving cases with **additional environmental safeguards** — **maximum 30 years**.
- Mechanism: **new para 9(iva)**, modelled on the mining-sector template. Draft (May 2026) had proposed **15 years**.
- Baseline for comparison: EIA 2006 sets validity by sector — e.g. **river valley** projects 10 years, **mining** up to 30 years (project life as assessed by the EAC).

**Notebook:** GS3 — Environment (environmental impact assessment; conservation and infrastructure trade-offs).

**Static anchor:** **Shankar IAS — Environmental Impact Assessment** chapter. Update the EIA-validity table with a fresh "ports/harbours/dredging: 20 (+5+5)" row and date-stamp it. Add a cross-link to the **CRZ Notification, 2019** (ports are a *coastal* clearance story as much as an EIA one) and to the **Great Nicobar** case-study card. In the Polity notebook, cross-link to **NGT** as the appellate forum against clearances under the NGT Act, 2010.

articles.title: Ministry of Heavy Industries: European Parliament's ITRE Committee delegation holds industrial-cooperation talks in New Delhi
articles.text:
**What it is.** On **22 September 2026**, Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel **H. D. Kumaraswamy** held talks with an **eight-member delegation of the European Parliament's Committee on Industry, Research and Energy (ITRE)**, including MEPs **Raffaele Stancanelli** and **Angelika Winzig**. The discussion covered **industrial development, clean energy, electric mobility and industrial decarbonisation**.

**Why it matters.** This is the industrial-policy follow-through on the India–EU relationship after the conclusion of **FTA negotiations at the India–EU Summit earlier in 2026**. The substantive ask on India's side is **European participation in battery manufacturing** — a sector where India's **Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC)** ambitions still depend on imported cell technology. Note also the decarbonisation angle: EU instruments such as **CBAM** make "greening" Indian steel a trade-access question, not only a climate one.

**Key facts.**
- **ITRE** is the European Parliament's standing committee on **industry, research and energy**.
- Indian schemes highlighted: **PLI for Automobiles and Auto Components**, **PLI for Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage**, and **PM E-DRIVE** for the EV ecosystem.
- **Global bidding for 10 GWh of ACC manufacturing capacity** is open, with a bid deadline of **13 October 2026**; European industry was invited to participate.
- Steel-sector cooperation discussed through **recycling and circular-economy** routes ("greening" of steel).
- Context: the **India–EU Summit of January 2026** concluded FTA negotiations and adopted a broader strategic-partnership agenda.

**Destination notebook:** GS3 — Economy (industrial policy, EV/battery manufacturing); cross-tag GS2 International Relations (India–EU).

articles.title: Ministry of Commerce & Industry: India–New Zealand FTA to enter into force on 20 October 2026
articles.text:
**What it is.** The India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, signed on **27 April 2026** at Bharat Mandapam by Commerce & Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and New Zealand's Trade Minister Todd McClay, will **enter into force on 20 October 2026 (Vijaya Dashami)**. Both sides completed internal processes; the New Zealand Parliament passed the enabling legislation on **16 September 2026**. The date was announced jointly by the two ministers on 21 September.

**Why it matters.** This is India's newest FTA with a developed economy, and the template is the one UPSC keeps returning to: full market access on the export side, hard carve-outs on agriculture and dairy, and services/mobility as the real prize. It also operationalises the **India–New Zealand Strategic Partnership: Roadmap to 2030**, announced during PM Modi's **July 2026 visit to New Zealand — the first by an Indian PM in four decades**.

**Key facts and figures**
- **Goods (India's gains):** every tariff line covering **100% of India's exports** to New Zealand becomes duty-free from day one; New Zealand's peak tariffs of **up to 10%** are eliminated. Immediate gainers — textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, processed foods. India also gets duty-free inputs: wooden logs, coking coal, metal scrap.
- **Agricultural protection (India's carve-outs):** **dairy, animal meat (except sheep), key agricultural commodities, sugar and edible oils excluded** from tariff concessions.
- **Calibrated access for NZ:** apples, kiwifruit and **Manuka honey** get access only through **Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQs) with a Minimum Import Price and seasonal import windows**, plus safeguards.
- **Agriculture Productivity Partnership:** dedicated Action Plans for kiwifruit, apples and honey; **Centres of Excellence** for orchard management, post-harvest practices, supply chains, food safety and sustainable beekeeping; a **Joint Agriculture Productivity Council** to monitor that market access is matched by cooperation.
- **Investment:** New Zealand commits to facilitate **USD 20 billion** of investment into India (agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure, start-ups).
- **Services & mobility:** access across roughly **118 sectors** (IT, professional services, audio-visual, construction, tourism); **MFN treatment locked in across about 139 sub-sectors**; **5,000 Temporary Employment Entry visas** a year for skilled Indians and **1,000 Working Holiday visas** a year for young Indians; **uncapped student mobility** with post-study work rights of **up to 3 years for STEM graduates and 4 years for doctoral scholars**.
- **Pharma:** New Zealand will accept inspection approvals from **US FDA, EMA, UK MHRA and Health Canada**, cutting market-entry time for Indian pharma and medical devices.
- **Trade base:** bilateral merchandise trade was about **USD 1.1 billion in 2025-26**; aspirational goal of doubling two-way goods and services trade to **NZ$7 billion (~₹35,000 crore) by 2030**.

**Destination notebook:** GS2 (International Relations — India's bilateral trade diplomacy) with a cross-entry in GS3 (Economy — external sector, FTAs and agricultural sensitivity).

articles.title: Six Chief Ministers sign the Kishau agreement — a 232.6-metre dam on the Tons, and a dispute settled without a tribunal — Polity & Governance
articles.text:
**The headline.** On **15 September 2026** the Chief Ministers of **Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Delhi and Haryana** signed the agreement on the long-pending **Kishau Multipurpose Project** in the upper Yamuna basin — a project surveyed and argued over for decades, now cleared of its political and cost-sharing obstacle but not of its clearances.

**The exam angle.** This is the cleanest available illustration of a theme UPSC returns to: India increasingly settles inter-State river water disputes by **negotiated agreement rather than tribunal adjudication**. Water is a State subject (Entry 17, State List), but the Union holds Entry 56 of the Union List over inter-State rivers, and Article 262 lets Parliament provide for adjudication *and* oust the courts. A signed agreement short-circuits all of it. The second angle is the *quality of the record*: environmental researchers have flagged unexplained discrepancies in the project's own official documents, which is a rare, citable example for a Mains answer on environmental governance.

**Key facts to memorise.**

- **River:** the **Tons**, the **largest tributary of the Yamuna**, flowing along the **Uttarakhand–Himachal Pradesh** border. The Yamuna rises at **Yamunotri** and joins the Ganga at Prayagraj.
- **Dam:** a **concrete gravity dam**, **232.6 m** — among India's tallest. (**Tehri**, ~260 m, remains the tallest.)
- **Design figures:** storage **1,562 MCM**; irrigation **97,000 hectares**; **1,476 million units** of hydropower.
- **Funding:** declared a **national project** — the Centre bears about **90%** of the cost, the States the remaining **10%**. Cost estimated in media reports at **₹15,000–15,624 crore** (the MHA statement gave no figure).
- **The swap worth remembering:** **Himachal Pradesh's water share goes to Delhi and Rajasthan**; in return those two bear the cost of Himachal's share of the *electricity* component.
- **Parent instrument:** the **12 May 1994 Upper Yamuna agreement**, which provided that a *separate agreement* would be signed for each storage project. An **in-principle** agreement among the six States was reached on **16 June 2026**.
- **Government claim:** about **25% of the Yamuna's water** would become available as **environmental flow**; the MHA describes this as the **tenth** water dispute taken up for resolution in the present tenure.
- **The discrepancies (excellent Mains material):** installed capacity listed as **422 MW** in the Environment Ministry's **47th Expert Appraisal Committee** document (January 2026) but **660 MW** in the 2018 HPPCL record and the **29th EAC** agenda (June 2022). Submergence is constant at **2,950 ha**, but the 2018 record showed **2,438 ha of forest** while the 2026 EAC document lists only **689 ha** — the status of the missing **1,749 ha** is unexplained.
- **Displacement:** **5,498 people from 701 families**, a figure derived from a **2014 field study and a 2018 report**, not re-verified (Himdhara Environmental Research and Action Collective).
- **The objection:** **SANDRP** (Himanshu Thakkar) argues the Himalaya is seismically unstable and that a dam of this height carries disproportionate risk; he calls the Yamuna-cleaning claim misleading, since regulating flow *dilutes* pollution rather than removing it.
- **Still pending:** Union Cabinet approval; **forest land diversion** under the **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam** (the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 as amended in 2023); **environmental clearance** under the **EIA Notification, 2006**; and a rehabilitation plan under the **LARR Act, 2013**.

**Destination notebook:** GS2 — Polity & Governance (federalism, inter-State relations); cross-tag GS3 — Environment & Infrastructure.

**Static anchor:** **Laxmikanth — "Inter-State Relations" chapter**, the section on Inter-State Water Disputes (Article 262, ISRWD Act 1956, River Boards Act 1956). *Nudge:* on that page, add a margin line — "**2026: Kishau — six-State negotiated agreement, no tribunal**" — next to your list of tribunals, and cross-link to the **Yamuna drainage system** page in your NCERT/GC Leong physical geography notes (Tons as largest Yamuna tributary; Lakhwar–Vyasi–Dakpathar–Asan cascade downstream).

articles.title: Ministry of Law and Justice: President appoints 14 judicial officers as Judges and Additional Judges of four High Courts
articles.text:
**What it is.** In exercise of the power conferred by the Constitution and **after consultation with the Chief Justice of India**, the President has appointed **14 judicial officers** as Judges/Additional Judges of the **Delhi**, **Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh**, **Jharkhand** and **Karnataka** High Courts. **Five of the 14 are women.** All 14 come from the **District Judiciary** — this is the "service quota" route to the High Court bench, not elevation from the Bar.

**Why it matters.** Straightforward prelims material on **Articles 217 and 224**, and useful Mains material on two live debates: **judicial appointments** (the collegium, the unsettled Memorandum of Procedure, and the perennial question of pendency versus vacancies) and **diversity on the bench**. Note the structural point the notification illustrates: a High Court bench is filled from **two streams** — advocates from the Bar and members of the **State Judicial Service** — and the composition of any batch tells you which stream the collegium is drawing on. Note also the constitutional anomaly on display: an **Additional Judge** under **Article 224** is appointed for a **fixed term not exceeding two years** to clear temporary arrears, a device that has become near-routine and is criticised for creating a probationary tier of judges whose confirmation depends on later executive and collegium action.

**Key facts and figures**

- **Total appointed:** 14 judicial officers across **four High Courts**; **five women** among them.
- **Delhi High Court:** **Smt. Nivedita Anil Sharma** and **Smt. Nisha Sahay Saxena** as **Judges**; **Sanjay Sharma, Bharat Parashar, Dr. (Smt.) Aditi Choudhary, Dinesh Bhatt** and **Arun Bhardwaj** as **Additional Judges**.
- **J&K and Ladakh High Court:** **Yash Paul Bourney** as a **Judge**.
- **Jharkhand High Court:** **Manoj Prasad, Akhil Kumar** and **Ram Sharma** as **Judges**.
- **Karnataka High Court:** **Smt. Usharani, K.S. Bharath Kumar** and **Smt. Nerale V. Bhavani** as **Additional Judges**.
- **Issued by:** Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice (notification signed by Narayan Prasad, Director).

**Constitutional anchors to revise alongside this**

- **Article 214** — a High Court for each State; **Article 231** — a common High Court for two or more States/UTs (the **J&K and Ladakh High Court** is the common High Court for the **UT of Jammu & Kashmir and the UT of Ladakh**; the **Delhi High Court** exists under the **Delhi High Court Act, 1966**).
- **Article 216** — composition: a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may from time to time deem necessary (**no fixed strength**).
- **Article 217** — appointment: by the **President**, after consultation with the **CJI**, the **Governor of the State**, and (for judges other than the Chief Justice) the **Chief Justice of that High Court**. **Qualifications:** citizen of India **and** either ten years' judicial office in India **or** ten years as an advocate of a High Court. **No minimum age is prescribed.** **Retirement age: 62 years.**
- **Article 224** — **Additional Judges** (temporary increase in business/arrears, for a period **not exceeding two years**) and **Acting Judges**. **Article 224A** — retired judges sitting at sittings of a High Court.
- **Article 222** — transfer of a judge from one High Court to another. **Article 218 read with 124(4)** — removal, on the Supreme Court judge's grounds and procedure.
- **Collegium:** not in the text of the Constitution — evolved through the **Second Judges Case (1993)** and **Third Judges Case (1998)**; the **99th Amendment and the NJAC Act were struck down in the Fourth Judges Case (2015)**.

**Notebook:** GS2 Polity (judiciary, appointment of High Court judges, collegium, separation of powers).

articles.title: Supreme Court asks the Centre to defer the mandatory third language for Class 6 to 2027 — Society
articles.text:
**Headline.** On **17 September 2026**, a three-judge Bench headed by **Chief Justice of India Surya Kant**, hearing petitions challenging **CBSE circulars** that advanced the mandatory **three-language requirement for Class 6 to the 2026-27 session**, urged the Centre and the Board to **defer implementation by a year to the 2027 academic year**, observing that enforcing the requirement **mid-term** imposes avoidable logistical strain on young children and their families. The Court did not strike the policy down; it pressed for a **transitional** approach, including making the requirement optional for the current year.

**Exam angle.** Three clean hooks. First, the **three-language formula** itself — it originates in the **National Education Policy of 1968** (drawing on the **Kothari Commission, 1964-66**), is restated in **NEP 1986** and in **NEP 2020**, and under NEP 2020 carries the explicit rider that **no language will be imposed on any State** and that at least two of the three should be **native to India**. Second, the **constitutional-federal** layer: **education is in the Concurrent List** (moved there by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**, Entry 25), so a national policy binds only through adoption and through central boards like CBSE — which is precisely why CBSE circulars, not a statute, are what is being litigated. Third, and this is the judicially interesting part: the Court is not adjudicating the **validity** of the policy but the **reasonableness of its transition** — a **legitimate-expectation / proportionality-in-implementation** argument rather than a substantive challenge. That distinction is worth a sentence in any Mains answer on judicial review of policy.

**Facts to memorise.**

- **Date and forum:** **17 September 2026**; Supreme Court, three-judge Bench headed by **CJI Surya Kant**; challenge to **CBSE** circulars advancing the Class 6 three-language mandate to **2026-27**; Court suggested deferral to **2027**.
- **Three-language formula:** first formalised in the **National Policy on Education, 1968**, following the **Kothari Commission (1964-66)**; reaffirmed in **NEP 1986** and **NEP 2020**.
- **NEP 2020 language provisions:** mother tongue/local language as medium of instruction **at least till Grade 5, preferably till Grade 8**; **three-language formula continues**, with **no language imposed on any State**, and **at least two of the three native to India**.
- **Constitutional frame:** **Education — Concurrent List, Entry 25**, shifted from the State List by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**. **Article 350A** — facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for linguistic minorities. **Article 351** — duty of the Union to promote the spread of Hindi. **Article 343** — Hindi in Devanagari as the official language of the Union; **Official Languages Act, 1963** for continued use of English.
- **Eighth Schedule** currently lists **22 languages** (14 at commencement; **Sindhi** added by the **21st Amendment, 1967**; **Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali** by the **71st Amendment, 1992**; **Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali** by the **92nd Amendment, 2003**).
- **CBSE** is a **board of the Ministry of Education**, not a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament — relevant to why the challenge is by writ against circulars.

**Notebook.** GS1 — Society (social empowerment, education, linguistic diversity) and GS2 — Governance (issues relating to development and management of the education sector; Centre-State relations).

**Static anchor.** Your **NEP 2020 note** plus **Laxmikanth, Chapter on Official Language (Part XVII, Articles 343-351)**. *Update:* add a three-line history of the **three-language formula (1968 → 1986 → 2020)** to the NEP note, and cross-link it to the **Official Language chapter** and to the **Concurrent List / 42nd Amendment** entry — the language question is simultaneously a policy, a federalism and a fundamental-rights topic, and UPSC has approached it from all three.

articles.title: Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of Commerce): 25th Meeting of SCO Ministers responsible for Foreign Economic and Trade Activities, Dushanbe
articles.text:
**What it is.** The **25th Meeting of Ministers of SCO Member States Responsible for Foreign Economic and Trade Activities** was held in **Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on 17 September 2026**, chaired by **Abdurahmon Abdurahmonzoda**, Tajikistan's Minister of Economic Development and Trade. **India was represented by Shri Yashvir Singh, Additional Secretary, Department of Commerce.** The Ministers agreed on the **"Action Plan for 2026–2030 for the Implementation of the Programme of Multilateral Trade and Economic Cooperation of the SCO Member States"**, to be placed before the **SCO Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers)** for approval.

**Why it matters.** The SCO's economic pillar is where India's position is most distinctive — and most constrained. India pressed the familiar **three pillars of "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity"** (the formulation PM Modi used at the SCO Summit in Bishkek) and emphasised **digital and cross-border payments** and **trade finance for MSMEs and start-ups**, which is India's comparative-advantage pitch (UPI-style rails) inside a grouping whose connectivity agenda is otherwise dominated by China's Belt and Road framing — an initiative India has consistently declined to endorse in SCO documents on sovereignty grounds relating to CPEC. Remember the institutional split: the **Council of Heads of State (CHS)** is the summit-level body, while trade and economic programmes such as this Action Plan are cleared by the **Council of Heads of Government (CHG)**.

**Key facts and figures**

- **Meeting:** 25th Meeting of SCO Ministers responsible for Foreign Economic and Trade Activities, **Dushanbe, 17 September 2026**.
- **India's representative:** Shri **Yashvir Singh**, Additional Secretary, Department of Commerce.
- **Main outcome:** agreement on the **Action Plan 2026–2030** implementing the SCO Programme of Multilateral Trade and Economic Cooperation; to be approved by the **CHG**.
- **India's emphases:** intra-SCO trade, lower trade costs, resilient supply chains, connectivity; **digital and cross-border payments**; **trade finance for MSMEs and start-ups**.
- **India's framing:** the **"Security, Connectivity, Opportunity"** triad.
- **SCO basics for revision:** founded **2001** (from the Shanghai Five of 1996); **Secretariat in Beijing**; **RATS (Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure) in Tashkent**; India and Pakistan joined as full members in **2017**, Iran in **2023**, Belarus in **2024**.

**Notebook:** GS2 International Relations (regional groupings, India and SCO, connectivity) + GS3 Economy (trade facilitation, supply chains).

articles.title: "Guidelines that exist only on paper" — the Supreme Court orders RBI to make its loan-recovery rules bite — Polity & Governance
articles.text:
**Headline.** In **Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.** (**2026 INSC 998**, judgment reported **16–17 September 2026**), a Bench of **Justices P. S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** held that a truck driver whose hypothecated vehicle was seized at about **1 a.m.** by breaking the steering lock, without the contractually required seven-day notice and without a signed possession memorandum, had been **arbitrarily deprived of his livelihood in violation of Articles 14 and 21**. The Court awarded **₹10 lakh compensation** plus refund of the ₹4.5 lakh sale price with 6% interest and ₹50,000 costs — and **directed the RBI to take effective steps to secure genuine compliance** by NBFCs and scheduled commercial banks with its recovery guidelines, master circulars and clarifications, which it said "have existed only on paper".

**Exam angle.** Three separable hooks, and this is the kind of judgment UPSC likes precisely because it is not about striking anything down. First, **Article 21 and the right to livelihood** — the Court applies *Olga Tellis* to a private financier's self-help repossession, which is an instructive extension of horizontal application through a regulated entity. Second, **the regulator's duty to enforce, not merely to issue** — RBI directions under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** have statutory force (*Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI*, 2020), so non-enforcement is itself a regulatory failure; this is a ready-made line on the gap between **rule-making and rule-enforcement capacity** in Indian regulation. Third, the Court's careful **refusal to condemn self-help repossession as such** — it said such clauses are "what make it commercially feasible" to lend against the financed asset to borrowers with no conventional collateral. That balance (financial inclusion vs. borrower dignity) is the quotable Mains line.

**Facts to memorise.**

- **Case:** *Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.*, **Neutral Citation 2026 INSC 998**; Bench — **Justices P. S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe**; appeal from the **Allahabad High Court**, which had dismissed the writ petition on delay.
- **Financier:** Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company Ltd. (an **NBFC**); loan repayable in **75 monthly instalments**, secured by **hypothecation**.
- **Relief:** loan accounts closed; **₹4.50 lakh** sale price refunded with **6% p.a.** interest; **₹10 lakh** compensation for mental agony and loss of livelihood; **₹50,000** costs. The completed sale was **not** undone.
- **Constitutional holding:** arbitrary, unnotified night-time seizure depriving a person of livelihood violates **Articles 14 and 21**.
- **Regulatory hook:** **Section 35A, Banking Regulation Act, 1949** — RBI directions have statutory force; **RBI Fair Practices Code** and master circulars (2008–2015) on recovery agents, debt-collection hours, privacy, grievance redressal and the **BCSBI Code**.
- **Precedents relied on:** ***ICICI Bank Ltd. v. Prakash Kaur* (2007)** — banks cannot employ "goondas" to seize vehicles; ***Orix Auto Finance (India) Ltd. v. Jagmander Singh* (2006)** and ***Sundaram Finance Ltd. v. T. Thankam* (2015)** — repossession is a contractual right unless unconscionable or against public policy.
- **Operative direction:** RBI to secure genuine compliance; the Registry was directed to send RBI a copy of the judgment.

**Notebook.** GS2 — Polity & Governance (Fundamental Rights, judicial review, regulatory bodies); usable in GS3 — Economy (NBFC regulation, financial inclusion).

**Static anchor.** **Laxmikanth — Chapter 7, Fundamental Rights**, the Article 21 sub-section. *Update:* append this case to your **Article 21 expansion ladder** (*Maneka Gandhi* 1978 → *Olga Tellis* 1985 → *Francis Coralie Mullin* → *Puttaswamy* 2017 → this) with the one-line tag "livelihood vs. self-help repossession", and cross-link to the **RBI/regulators page** in Mrunal Pillar 1 under "Fair Practices Code / recovery agents".

articles.title: The monsoon starts to leave — withdrawal from West Rajasthan around 19 September, with the season 15% short — Geography
articles.text:
**Headline.** The **India Meteorological Department** said on **14 September 2026** that conditions are becoming favourable for the **withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from parts of West Rajasthan around 19 September 2026** — the start of the retreat from the Indian mainland, **about two days later than the normal date of 17 September**. Cumulative rainfall from **1 June to 13 September** stands at **15% below normal**, with the **South Peninsula worst hit at −28%**.

**Exam angle.** Two things to extract. First, the **withdrawal sequence itself is standard Prelims material** and it is the mirror image of onset: the monsoon **arrives** at Kerala around **1 June** and moves north-west, and it **withdraws** from **extreme north-west India (West Rajasthan) first**, around 17 September, retreating south-east and clearing the mainland by around **15 October** — a **gradual** retreat, unlike the abrupt "burst" of onset. Second, this year is a textbook case of **why seasonal totals mislead**: June was **−36.5%**, July was **+1%**, and the season still ends near −15% with huge regional spread (−28% in the South Peninsula, −6% in Central India). Pair that with the **reservoir number** — 129.87 BCM against a ten-year average of 134.23 BCM and last year's 159.18 BCM — and you have a complete rabi-sowing and drinking-water argument without needing any additional source.

**Facts to memorise.**

- **Withdrawal onset:** around **19 September 2026** from parts of **West Rajasthan**; IMD's **normal date for the start of withdrawal is 17 September** (revised in 2020 from the earlier 1 September); complete withdrawal from the country normally by around **15 October**.
- **Season so far (1 June – 13 September 2026):** all-India **−15%**; **South Peninsula −28%**, **East & North-East India −25%**, **North-West India −10%**, **Central India −6%**.
- **Month-by-month:** **June −36.5%**, **July +1%**, recovery in July–August narrowing the deficit to about 15%.
- **Agriculture:** kharif acreage had lagged about **21%** by end-June; by **11 September** total acreage was about **1.45% below last year** and **0.72% below the five-year normal**. Laggards: **urad, moong, soybean, cotton**.
- **Reservoirs (as on 3 September 2026):** **129.87 BCM** across the **178** monitored reservoirs, against **159.18 BCM** last year and a ten-year average of **134.23 BCM**.
- **Static frame:** IMD defines withdrawal by **cessation of rain for about five days, establishment of anticyclonic circulation and a marked drop in moisture**; the retreat is accompanied by **"October heat"** (high temperature with high humidity) and the onset of the **north-east / retreating monsoon**, which brings the main rains to the **Coromandel Coast**, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Kerala in **October–December**.

**Notebook.** GS1 — Geography (Indian climate, monsoon mechanism); GS3 — Agriculture and Disaster Management (drought, reservoir storage).

**Static anchor.** **NCERT Class XI, *India: Physical Environment*, Chapter 4 — Climate** (and Goh Cheng Leong's monsoon chapter). *Update:* on your monsoon page, write the **onset and withdrawal dates side by side as two arrows** (onset: Kerala 1 June → NW India 8 July, south-east to north-west; withdrawal: West Rajasthan 17 September → mainland clear by 15 October, north-west to south-east), and cross-link it to the **north-east monsoon** note so the "which coast gets rain in which season" question never costs you a mark.

articles.title: The World Circular Economy Forum opens in Gandhinagar — its 10th edition and its first in South Asia — Environment
articles.text:
**Headline.** WCEF 2026 runs **15–18 September at Mahatma Mandir, Gandhinagar**, on the theme *"Circular economy: Transition for people and prosperity"* — convened by Finland's **Sitra** with the **Central Pollution Control Board**, supported by MoEFCC and the Gujarat government. Over 2,000 participants from 65-plus countries; 125-plus exhibitors. The Board of the **10-Year Framework of Programmes on Sustainable Consumption and Production (10YFP)** meets at Gandhinagar on 15 September, with India having recently taken over as **Co-Chair**.

**Exam angle.** Circularity is the connective tissue between SDG 12, the plastics-treaty negotiations, critical-mineral security and Mission LiFE — a single Mains paragraph can carry all four. The examiner's favourite distinction is **recycling (end-of-pipe, still linear) vs circularity (design-stage: durability, repairability, reuse, remanufacture)**, and the Indian policy instrument that operationalises it is **Extended Producer Responsibility**, which UPSC has already asked about directly.

**Facts to memorise.**

- WCEF launched by **Sitra (the Finnish Innovation Fund) at Helsinki in 2017**; 2026 is the **10th edition**, the first in South Asia.
- **10YFP** — the SCP framework adopted at **Rio+20 (2012)**, secretariat with UNEP; India now Co-Chair of its Board.
- India's architecture: **NITI Aayog's 11 circular-economy committees (March 2021)** across municipal solid and liquid waste, scrap metal, Li-ion batteries, tyres and rubber, gypsum, end-of-life vehicles, e-waste, hazardous industrial waste, used oil, agricultural waste and solar panels.
- EPR is embedded in the **Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022)**, **E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022** and **Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** — but was *first introduced* in the **e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011**.

**Notebook.** GS3 — Environment (Pollution & waste management) with a GS3 Economy spillover on resource security.

**Static anchor.** Shankar IAS *Environment* — Pollution / Waste Management chapter. *Update:* add the 11 NITI focus sectors as a memorised list, and cross-link EPR to the three waste rules plus the 2019 PYQ.

articles.title: Places in News: Perim Island falls, and one actor now sits astride both of the Arabian Peninsula's chokepoints — Geography
articles.text:
**Headline:** Houthi (Ansar Allah) forces took the port city of **Mokha** and then, on **11 September 2026**, **Perim Island** — the islet that splits the **Bab el-Mandeb** strait into two navigable channels — after government forces withdrew, giving them **the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coastline**. Saudi Arabia separately shut a major oil pipeline following a drone attack.

**Exam angle:** UPSC's "Places in News" habit is to ask what a feature **connects**, not who controls it — so fix the geography first and treat the politics as context. **Bab el-Mandeb** ("Gate of Tears") separates **Yemen** on the Arabian Peninsula from **Djibouti and Eritrea** in the Horn of Africa, and links the **Red Sea** to the **Gulf of Aden**, and through it to the **Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean**. It is the *southern* gate of the **Suez** route; the *northern* gate is the **Strait of Gubal / Gulf of Suez**. The strategic significance of this particular week is that a single aligned network now has coercive reach over **both Bab el-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz** — the two chokepoints that bracket the Arabian Peninsula. That matters asymmetrically: Hormuz has a **partial land bypass** (Saudi Arabia's East–West pipeline to Yanbu, the UAE's Fujairah pipeline), whereas **Bab el-Mandeb has none** — disruption simply forces the long haul around the **Cape of Good Hope**, adding roughly 8–10 days and a large freight-and-insurance premium to India–Europe cargo. India's exposure is direct: a large share of India's westbound trade and refined-product exports to Europe transits Red Sea–Suez, and the **Indian Navy's Operation Sankalp** presence in the region exists precisely for this. Bolt on the **India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC)** as the structural counter-argument: IMEC's rationale is partly that it offers a Suez-independent route to Europe.

**Facts to memorise:**

- **Bab el-Mandeb:** connects the **Red Sea** ↔ **Gulf of Aden** (→ Arabian Sea, Indian Ocean). Separates **Yemen** from **Djibouti and Eritrea**. About **30 km** at its narrowest; **Perim Island** (Yemeni) splits it into two channels and has its own airstrip.
- **Traffic:** roughly **one-tenth of global seaborne oil trade** and about **a quarter of global container trade**; the world's **third-busiest oil chokepoint** after **Hormuz** and **Malacca**.
- **No land bypass exists** for Bab el-Mandeb, unlike Hormuz. Alternative = **Cape of Good Hope**.
- **Suez Canal** opened **1869**; **nationalised by Egypt in 1956** (Suez Crisis); it is the only sea route between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean that avoids circumnavigating Africa.
- **Littoral states of the Red Sea:** Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti (via Bab el-Mandeb), Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Jordan and Israel (via the **Gulf of Aqaba**).
- **Nearby features often confused:** the **Hanish Islands** (Yemen–Eritrea dispute, arbitrated 1998); **Socotra** (Yemeni, in the Arabian Sea, a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**); **Djibouti**, which hosts foreign military bases including China's first overseas base.
- **India's presence:** **Operation Sankalp** (since June 2019, Gulf of Oman/Persian Gulf); the **Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR)** at **Gurugram** (2018); India is a full member of the **Combined Maritime Forces**, Bahrain.

**Notebook:** GS1 — Geography (important geophysical phenomena; world map/places in news), with GS2 (IR) and GS3 (economy, energy security) spillovers.

**Static anchor:** **NCERT Class XI *Fundamentals of Physical Geography* / the world-map section of your atlas work, plus your "Straits and Chokepoints" one-pager.** *Update:* on your chokepoints page, add a **two-column comparison of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb** — width, share of oil trade, whether a land bypass exists, and which flank of the Arabian Peninsula each guards. Mark **Perim, Socotra, the Hanish Islands, Mokha, Hodeidah and Djibouti** on your West Asia map. **Cross-link** to **IMEC** and to your **Indian Ocean Region security** note.

articles.title: Acharya Vinoba Bhave's birth anniversary — the land-reform movement that worked morally and failed statistically — Modern History
articles.text:
**Headline:** The Prime Minister paid tribute to **Acharya Vinoba Bhave** on his **birth anniversary (11 September)** — born **Vinayak Narahari Bhave, 11 September 1895 – 15 November 1982** — the Gandhian who was hand-picked as India's **first individual Satyagrahi in 1940** and who launched the **Bhoodan movement in 1951**.

**Exam angle:** This is a **post-independence GS1 topic** that UPSC has asked in Mains verbatim (see the PYQ mirror), and the examinable argument is the gap between **moral success and structural failure**. Bhoodan was a **voluntary, non-legislative** alternative to state-led land redistribution: Bhave walked village to village asking landowners to gift land, and from **1954** escalated to **Gramdan**, the donation of whole villages into common ownership. The movement collected roughly **42 lakh acres**, but only a fraction was ever distributed — much of it was **litigated, uncultivable, or reverted** when Gramdan villages drifted back to individual title. The reason to know the numbers is that they let you make the argument precisely: voluntary transfer could not overcome **absentee landlordism, benami holdings and defective land records** — which is exactly the diagnosis that statutory **land-ceiling legislation** and, much later, **land-records digitisation** were meant to address. That gives you a live cross-link to **DILRMP 3.0** (12 September note). The second thread is **ideological**: Bhoodan is the practical arm of **Sarvodaya** and of Gandhi's **trusteeship** doctrine, and its political afterlife runs through **Jayaprakash Narayan**, who left party politics for Sarvodaya in 1954 and returned in 1974 with **Sampoorna Kranti** — a chain worth writing in one line.

**Facts to memorise:**

- **Vinayak Narahari "Vinoba" Bhave**, b. **11 September 1895**, Gagode village, **Raigad district, Maharashtra** (Konkan); d. 15 November 1982. Gandhi gave him the name **Vinoba**, placing him in the lineage of **Jnanoba and Tukoba**. Met Gandhi at **Ahmedabad, 7 June 1916**.
- **First individual Satyagrahi**, selected by Gandhi to launch the **Individual Civil Disobedience Movement, October 1940**; **Jawaharlal Nehru** was the second. Gandhi introduced him publicly through the essay ***"Who is Vinoba?"***
- **Bhoodan (land-gift) movement:** launched **18 April 1951** at **Pochampally village, Nalgonda district** (then Hyderabad State, now **Telangana**), where **Vedre Ramachandra Reddy** donated **100 acres** to landless Harijan families. **Gramdan** (village-gift) followed from **1954**; the first Gramdan village was **Mangroth (Uttar Pradesh)**.
- **Institutions:** **Sarva Seva Sangh** and the **Akhil Bharat Sarva Seva Sangh** carried the movement; **Gram Seva Mandal, Wardha (1934)**; earlier, the **Nagpur Flag Satyagraha (1923)**.
- **Writings:** ***Geetai*** (the Bhagavad Gita in Marathi verse, 1930–31); ***Gita Pravachane*** (18 talks delivered in **Dhule jail, 1932**); *Swarajya-Shastra*; *Sthitaprajna-Darshan*.
- **Honours:** first international **Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership (1958)**; **Bharat Ratna, posthumously in 1983**.
- **Contrast to hold ready:** Bhoodan = **voluntary and moral**; **land-ceiling laws** = **statutory and coercive**, and many were placed in the **Ninth Schedule** to shield them from judicial review.

**Notebook:** GS1 — Modern Indian History and post-independence consolidation (social reformers; land reforms), with a GS4 spillover (trusteeship, moral persuasion as an instrument of change).

**Static anchor:** **Spectrum / Bipan Chandra — the post-independence land-reforms section; NCERT Class XII *Politics in India Since Independence*, Ch. 3 ("Politics of Planned Development").** *Update:* build a single **land-reforms ladder** — *Zamindari abolition (1950s) → Tenancy reform → Bhoodan–Gramdan (1951/1954, voluntary) → Land-ceiling legislation + Ninth Schedule → Consolidation of holdings → DILRMP/SVAMITVA (records, 2008–)* — and mark against each whether it was **voluntary or statutory** and **why it under-delivered**. **Cross-link** to your **Ninth Schedule / *I.R. Coelho* (2007)** note in Laxmikanth and to the **DILRMP 3.0** entry from 12 September.

articles.title: Ministry of Science & Technology (DST–BSIP): Bakhira Lake sediments yield a 25,000-year monsoon record for the Central Ganga Plain
articles.text:
**What it is.** Researchers at the **Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP)**, an autonomous institute of the **Department of Science and Technology**, used **environmental magnetic properties** of sediments beneath **Bakhira Lake** (Sant Kabir Nagar, Uttar Pradesh) — combined with grain-size, geochemical and clay-mineralogical data — to reconstruct **Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM)** variability since the **Last Glacial Maximum**.

**Why it matters.** Long, high-resolution palaeoclimate records from the **Central Ganga Plain** are scarce and mostly confined to the Holocene. A well-dated 25,000-year archive improves **monsoon models** and, downstream, **water-resource management** in an intensely agricultural region.

**Key facts and figures**

- **Bakhira Lake** lies in the **Ghaghara–Rapti alluvial system** and is a perennial **oxbow/floodplain wetland** formed by the migration and cut-off of the **Rapti River**. One of **Uttar Pradesh's largest wetlands**, it was designated a **Ramsar Site in 2022**.
- The sequence extends to about **25 ka**, constrained by **seven AMS radiocarbon dates**.
- Climatic intervals identified: **Last Glacial Maximum / Heinrich Stadial 1** (~25.3–18.1 cal ka BP, cold-dry, weak ISM); **Bølling–Allerød** (~15.3–12.8 cal ka BP, warm-humid, enhanced ISM); **Younger Dryas** (~12.8–11.1 cal ka BP, cooling and weakened monsoon); **Holocene Climatic Optimum** (~9.2–4 cal ka BP, warm-wet, enhanced precipitation); **late Holocene droughts** (~4–2 cal ka BP).
- Published in *Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology*.

**Notebook:** GS1 Geography (monsoon, fluvial geomorphology) / GS3 Environment (wetlands, climate).

---

### Also worth a line (9–10 September 2026)

Reiterated that increasing the **carbon sink is India's third NDC target** under the UNFCCC, that **FSI** has done **biennial assessments since 1987** through the **India State of Forest Report**, and that India's enhanced ambition is a **3.5–4.0 billion tonne CO₂-equivalent carbon sink by 2035**.

articles.title: Rani Avantibai Lodhi gets a statue in Lucknow — the 1857 revolt beyond the four famous names — Modern History
articles.text:
**Headline.** Defence Minister **Rajnath Singh**, with UP Chief Minister **Yogi Adityanath**, unveiled a statue of **Veerangana Rani Avantibai Lodhi** in **Lucknow on 30 August 2026**, drawing a line from the 1857 warrior queens to women officers who flew combat roles in Operation Sindoor.

**Exam angle.** UPSC's 1857 questions have moved steadily away from Delhi–Kanpur–Lucknow and toward **regional centres and their leaders** — exactly the space Avantibai occupies. Her case is also the textbook illustration of a **doctrine that is not the Doctrine of Lapse**: her husband died leaving **minor** heirs, so the Company did not annex Ramgarh outright — it placed the estate under the **Court of Wards** and installed *sarbarahkars* (superintendents), a mechanism used for minor or "incompetent" heirs. That is a distinction students routinely get wrong, and it is precisely the sort of thing a statement-based Prelims question exploits. Avantibai expelled the Company's administrators, called on cultivators to refuse British revenue demands, and coordinated with the **Gond ruler Raja Shankar Shah of Garha-Mandla** through the famous **bangle appeal** — glass bangles sent with letters to neighbouring chiefs and zamindars, taunting them to fight or accept the bangles. She won at the **Battle of Kheri** near Mandla against Deputy Commissioner Waddington in 1857, then shifted to guerrilla operations from the **Devhargarh** hills, and took her own life on **20 March 1858** at Sukhi-Talaiya rather than be captured. Her Mahakoshal base — Gond and farming country — is the entry point for the **tribal dimension of 1857**, which is separate from and usually more useful than the sepoy narrative.

**Facts to memorise.**

- **Maharani Avantibai Lodhi**, **16 August 1831 – 20 March 1858**; queen-regent of the estate of **Ramgarh** (present-day **Dindori and Mandla districts, Madhya Pradesh**); born at **Mankedi village, Seoni district**.
- Married **Raja Vikramaditya Singh of Ramgarh**; assumed regency for minor sons **Aman Singh** and **Sher Singh** when he was incapacitated.
- Mechanism of British seizure: **Court of Wards** with **sarbarahkars** — not the **Doctrine of Lapse** (which applied to rulers dying *without* a natural heir).
- Ally: **Raja Shankar Shah**, Gond ruler of **Garha-Mandla**, executed by the British at Jabalpur in **September 1857** along with his son **Raghunath Shah** (blown from a cannon).
- **The bangle appeal** — glass bangles sent with letters to neighbouring rulers and zamindars as a challenge to join the revolt.
- **Battle of Kheri** (near Mandla, late 1857) — roughly **4,000 troops** defeated the force under Deputy Commissioner **Waddington**.
- Retreat to the **Devhargarh** hills; guerrilla strikes; encircled at **Sukhi-Talaiya** between Balapur and Ramgarh; **martyrdom on 20 March 1858**, aged 27.
- Group her with the other *veeranganas*: **Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi)**, **Jhalkari Bai** (Lakshmibai's Durga Dal commander), **Begum Hazrat Mahal (Awadh)**, **Rani Durgavati** (16th-century Gond queen of Garha-Katanga — *not* 1857; a standard trap), **Uda Devi (Sikandar Bagh)**.
- Other 1857 centre-and-leader pairs to have cold: **Delhi — Bahadur Shah II / Bakht Khan; Kanpur — Nana Saheb / Tantia Tope; Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai; Bareilly — Khan Bahadur Khan; Bihar (Jagdishpur) — Kunwar Singh; Faizabad — Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah; Allahabad — Liaquat Ali; Assam — Kandarpeshwar Singha; Orissa (Sambalpur) — Surendra Sai.**

**Notebook:** GS1 — Modern History (the Revolt of 1857; significant personalities), with a GS1 Society cross-tag on women's participation in the freedom struggle.

**Static anchor:** **Spectrum — *A Brief History of Modern India*, "The Revolt of 1857"** chapter, plus the "Peasant and Tribal Uprisings" chapter for the Mahakoshal/Gond link. *Nudge: your 1857 centre-leader table almost certainly has six or seven rows. Extend it to twelve — add Ramgarh (Avantibai Lodhi), Garha-Mandla (Shankar Shah), Sambalpur (Surendra Sai), Faizabad (Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah) and Assam (Kandarpeshwar Singha) — and add a two-line box distinguishing the Doctrine of Lapse from the Court of Wards, since Ramgarh is a Court of Wards case, not a Lapse case.*

articles.title: Parliament passes the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill, 2026 — a 135-year-old colonial statute goes — Economy
articles.text:
**Headline:** The Rajya Sabha cleared the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill, 2026 on **10 August 2026** (Lok Sabha had passed it on 5 August), completing Parliamentary passage of a law that repeals and replaces the **Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891** and gives cloud-stored and digital bank records full evidentiary standing.

**Exam angle:** A quiet but genuinely high-yield item — it sits at the junction of GS3 Economy (banking, digital financial infrastructure) and GS2 (colonial-law repeal, ease of doing business). The larger story is India's evidence law catching up with a banking system where the "book" no longer exists physically: read it alongside the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023**, which already made electronic records admissible as *primary* evidence. Also a good Mains line on cutting litigation cost — banks no longer have to produce or prove physical ledgers in recovery and fraud proceedings, which matters for **DRTs, IBC proceedings and cyber-fraud prosecutions**.

**Facts to memorise:**

- Bill No. **147 of 2026**; introduced in Lok Sabha **3 August 2026**, passed LS **5 August**, passed RS **10 August 2026**. Repeals the **Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891**.
- **"Bankers' books" redefined** to cover ledgers, day-books, cash-books, account books and all records used in ordinary banking business, kept in **physical, electronic, digital or cloud-based** form — including **back-up and disaster-recovery sites**, onsite or offsite/virtual.
- Electronic/digital records are **admissible, valid and legally enforceable** subject to conditions: the system was in regular use and operating properly, no unauthorised alteration or tampering, and the network/devices were secured against cyber risk.
- **"Legal proceeding" widened** to include court proceedings, **arbitration**, and investigations/inquiries conducted under law for collection of evidence.
- **Retained safeguard:** a bank officer cannot be compelled to produce a banker's book, or appear as a witness to prove its contents, in a proceeding to which the bank is **not a party** — except by order of a court or judge made **for a special cause**.

**Notebook:** GS3 — Economy (Banking & Financial Sector Reform); cross-file in GS2 (Repeal of colonial laws)

**Static anchor:** **Mrunal — Pillar 3 (Banking / BFSI)**, banking-regulation sub-section. Add a short "evidence & recovery architecture" box, and **cross-link** it to your Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 note on Sections 61–63 (electronic records as primary evidence) so the two laws sit on one page.

articles.title: Hyderabad hosts the 2nd BRICS Anti-Corruption Working Group and Asset Recovery Expert Network — International Relations
articles.text:
**Headline:** The Department of Personnel and Training is hosting the second meeting of the **BRICS Anti-Corruption Working Group (ACWG)** and the second meeting of the **BRICS Expert Network on Asset Recovery** in Hyderabad on **4–5 August 2026**, under India's BRICS Chairship of 2026. Inauguration by DoPT Secretary Ms Rachna Shah.

**Exam angle:**
- India's BRICS Chairship year is a guaranteed GS2/IR theme; the examinable distinction is **which ministry is nodal for which BRICS track** — DoPT for anti-corruption, unlike the more familiar MEA/Finance-led tracks.
- This is the "economic-offender extradition and asset recovery" theme that UPSC likes to pair with **UNCAC (2003)**, the **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018**, and Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties. Note the agenda language: cooperation is **"informal"** — i.e. agency-to-agency channels that run *alongside*, not in place of, formal MLAT/extradition routes.
- The FinTech and digital-asset corruption-risk agenda is a fresh GS3 crossover (crypto, virtual digital assets, PMLA reporting entity obligations).

**Key facts / figures to memorise:**
- Theme of India's BRICS Chairship 2026: **"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability"**.
- Nodal department for the BRICS anti-corruption track in India: **DoPT, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions**.
- Three agenda pillars: (i) informal cooperation to **trace fugitive offenders** and support extradition; (ii) operational information-sharing through the **Expert Network on Asset Recovery**; (iii) corruption risks from **FinTech, digital assets and emerging digital financial instruments**.
- Side event on 5 August: **"Ethical Governance through Innovation and Tech-Driven Systems"** — digital public procurement, citizen engagement, transparency.
- Anchor treaty: **UN Convention against Corruption (UNCAC), 2003** — India signed in 2005, ratified in **2011**.

**Destination notebook:** GS2 — International Relations (Groupings & Agreements involving India); cross-file under GS4/GS2 Governance (probity, transparency).

**Static anchor:** *Laxmikanth* — chapters on the **CVC** and the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas**, plus your BRICS institutional note. **Update:** add a "BRICS working-group architecture under India's 2026 Chairship" line to the BRICS page, and cross-link the **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (as amended 2018)** and the **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018** from the anti-corruption page.

articles.title: Second meeting of the BRICS Anti-Corruption Working Group opens in Hyderabad
articles.text:
**Ministry:** Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (DoPT) | **Date:** 04 Aug 2026

articles.title: Rakhigarhi skeletons transferred to AnSI for ancient-DNA study
articles.text:
**Headline:** ASI formally handed Harappan skeletal remains from **Rakhigarhi (Haryana)** to the **Anthropological Survey of India (AnSI)** for advanced research.

**Exam angle (GS1 — Art & Culture/Ancient History):** Reinforces "Places in News" + Harappan civilisation + India's growing **ancient-DNA/bioarchaeology** capacity. Two premier Ministry of Culture bodies (ASI ↔ AnSI) under an MoU.

**Memorise:** Rakhigarhi = among the **largest Indus–Saraswati (Harappan)** settlements, in Haryana (Ghaggar plain). 2025–26 field season (ASI Excavation Branch-II) found **8 burials at Mound No. 7**; **3 complete skeletons** + fragments moved to AnSI's skeletal repository, **Kolkata**. Aim: ancestry, diet, health, migration via aDNA.

**Notebook:** GS1 — Ancient History / Art & Culture. **Static anchor:** Old NCERT *"Bricks, Beads and Bones"* / Nitin Singhania IVC chapter — add Rakhigarhi (largest site) and the AnSI ancient-DNA link.
